paragraphs: This paper studies how robots can learn useful skills from data that has already been collected, without manually designed rewards or further exploration during training. It frames understanding an environment in practical terms: learn how to reach goal states represented in the dataset. This turns past experience into material for learning a range of behaviors.

The method combines goal-conditioned Q-learning with hindsight relabeling, which reinterprets recorded experience in terms of goals it achieved. The authors also develop techniques specifically for the difficult offline setting. Their objective connects learning directly to what a robot can accomplish, while making it possible to reuse data without assigning a separate reward to every desired skill.

The reported results show learning from camera images on real robots, with skills generalizing to unseen objects and scenes. Goal chaining supports longer-horizon goals by connecting experience across multiple episodes. The learned representations can also help downstream tasks through pretraining or auxiliary objectives, giving the offline data value beyond the initially learned goal-reaching behaviors.
icml-2021-actionable-models-unsupervised.tldr: Robots learn goal-reaching skills and useful representations from existing data without manually specified rewards or additional exploration.

paragraphs: Classification with rejection lets a model decline to make a prediction when an error would be too costly. This paper develops that capability through cost-sensitive classification, where different mistakes receive different penalties. The motivation is to support decisions in settings such as diagnosis and inspection, where forcing a prediction can create avoidable risk.

The proposed method learns an ensemble of cost-sensitive classifiers. It can make rejection decisions without first estimating the probability of every class, which the authors connect to improved classification accuracy. The same approach accommodates binary and multiclass problems and permits a flexible selection of training losses, including non-convex ones, without complicated changes for each loss.

The theoretical justification applies to classification-calibrated losses, preserving a specific condition on the losses covered by the analysis. Experiments demonstrate usefulness with clean labels, noisy labels, and positive-unlabeled data. Together, these results position cost-sensitive learning as a flexible foundation for rejection, with both a theoretical rationale and evidence across several forms of supervision.
icml-2021-classification-with-rejection-.tldr: An ensemble of cost-sensitive classifiers learns when to reject predictions without requiring class-probability estimates.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization shared across a network of agents when the solution must lie on the Stiefel manifold. Each agent owns a smooth local objective, and together they minimize the sum of those objectives. Communication follows an undirected, connected graph. Both the potentially non-convex objectives and the non-convex constraint set make coordination more difficult.

The authors propose two decentralized methods that account for the geometry of the constraint. Their stochastic gradient method, DRSGD, has a convergence rate of O(1/√K) to a stationary point. Their gradient tracking method, DRGTA, achieves a rate of O(1/K) and supports exact convergence with a constant step size. These are stationary-point guarantees, rather than guarantees of finding a global optimum.

Both methods use multiple consensus steps to keep the iterates within a local region where agents remain sufficiently coordinated. The paper identifies DRGTA as the first decentralized algorithm providing exact convergence for this manifold-constrained distributed problem. Its contribution combines geometric optimization with communication mechanisms that sustain agreement among agents.
icml-2021-decentralized-riemannian-gradi.tldr: Two decentralized methods provide stationary-point convergence guarantees for distributed optimization on the Stiefel manifold.

paragraphs: Node embeddings compress a graph into low-dimensional representations, but successful downstream use does not explain exactly which graph properties survive that compression. This paper investigates the question by reversing the process. Starting from embeddings produced by a variant of DeepWalk, it asks whether a graph can be reconstructed that produces a similar representation.

The authors develop algorithms for accurate embedding inversion. The reconstruction target is a graph with embeddings close to the supplied ones, so matching the representation does not itself establish that the original graph has been recovered. Comparing the reconstructed graph with the original provides a way to examine which structural details the embedding retains or loses.

Experiments on real networks find that individual edges and broader properties such as triangle density are often lost, while community structure is often preserved or strengthened. These observations suggest that this embedding method can emphasize groups of related nodes without retaining detailed connectivity. The results help clarify what information may support learning tasks that use these representations.
icml-2021-deepwalking-backwards-from-emb.tldr: Inverting a DeepWalk variant reveals that similar embeddings can preserve communities while losing edges and other graph properties.

paragraphs: Spatial path planning requires choosing actions that account for obstacles and destinations. This paper learns a planner from data so that experience with past environments can inform future plans. The approach aims to exploit recurring spatial patterns instead of treating every planning problem as an entirely fresh optimization with a fully known map.

Spatial Planning Transformers generate actions from an obstacle map by reasoning over long-range spatial dependencies. This changes how information moves through the planner compared with learned methods that repeatedly propagate information through local convolutions. When the true map is unavailable, pretrained planners are incorporated into an end-to-end system with explicit mapper and planner components.

The authors report generalization to maps and goals outside the training distribution using this combined structure. Across the evaluated navigation and manipulation setups, SPTs outperform previous leading differentiable planners, with absolute improvements of 7–19%. These findings support long-range spatial reasoning and an explicit mapping-and-planning structure as useful ingredients for learned planning in the tested settings.
icml-2021-differentiable-spatial-plannin.tldr: Spatial Planning Transformers learn long-range spatial reasoning and improve differentiable planning across evaluated navigation and manipulation tasks.

paragraphs: Fair classification becomes harder when the protected attributes used to assess fairness contain errors. The paper addresses this setting with an optimization framework that learns a classifier despite noisy perturbations in those attributes. Its goal is to retain meaningful control over both predictive accuracy and fairness when the information defining protected groups is imperfect.

The framework supports a broad family of fairness requirements expressed as linear or linear-fractional constraints. It can also handle several protected attributes and attributes with more than two categories. This flexibility matters because fairness requirements and group definitions need not fit a single binary distinction. The resulting classifier comes with provable guarantees covering both accuracy and fairness.

On two real-world datasets, the authors report achieving either statistical-rate fairness or false-positive-rate fairness with only a small loss in accuracy, including under substantial noise. The empirical result concerns these tested fairness choices and datasets. It illustrates how the framework's broader optimization machinery can translate into useful accuracy–fairness tradeoffs when protected-attribute information is unreliable.
icml-2021-fair-classification-with-noisy.tldr: An optimization framework learns classifiers with accuracy and fairness guarantees despite noise in protected attributes.

paragraphs: Goal-conditioned reinforcement learning can support many skills, but goals requiring extended sequences of decisions remain difficult. This paper introduces imagined intermediate states to help train the policy. The central idea is to use plausible progress toward a distant goal as guidance for learning, without making the intermediate states compulsory destinations.

A separate high-level policy predicts states halfway toward the goal, using the value function to assess reachability. It is trained alongside the main policy and its critic. The predicted subgoals define a prior policy, which enters a policy-iteration procedure constrained by KL divergence. This prior is intended to regularize learning and help it proceed faster.

The subgoals are used during training only; at test time, the agent executes the learned policy without generating them. This separates the learning guidance from the deployed decision process. Evaluations on complex robotic navigation and manipulation tasks report a large improvement over existing methods, supporting the usefulness of imagined subgoals as training guidance in those tasks.
icml-2021-goal-conditioned-reinforcement.tldr: Imagined subgoals guide and regularize goal-conditioned policy training without being required during deployment.

paragraphs: GRAND treats learning on a graph as a continuous diffusion process. In this view, a graph neural network is a discrete implementation of an underlying partial differential equation. The perspective gives network design a mathematical foundation: choices about layers and graph topology correspond to choices about discretizing time and spatial operators.

This connection lets the authors develop a broad class of graph neural networks while explicitly considering problems such as depth, oversmoothing, and information bottlenecks. Rather than considering architecture choices in isolation, the framework relates them to the behavior of diffusion. Stability under perturbations of the input data is a central concern, addressed for both explicit and implicit discretization schemes.

The paper develops linear and nonlinear versions of GRAND and reports competitive performance on many standard graph benchmarks. The contribution therefore includes both a general design framework and concrete models tested within it. The reported findings support diffusion-based design as a useful approach to graph learning, without claiming that every graph-learning difficulty is universally resolved.
icml-2021-grand-graph-neural-diffusion-e.tldr: GRAND derives graph neural networks from continuous diffusion, linking architecture and stability to numerical discretization.

paragraphs: HoroPCA adapts principal component analysis to data in hyperbolic space. The paper starts from three ingredients of PCA: defining subspaces from directions, projecting data while retaining information along those directions, and measuring the variance captured by a projection. Each ingredient must be reconsidered for the geometry in which the data lives.

The proposed method generalizes these ingredients while centering the problem on extracting principal directions. The authors establish that this approach better preserves original information, including distances, than previous PCA generalizations in their theoretical analysis. This matters because reducing dimensionality is useful only to the extent that the smaller representation retains relationships needed for subsequent analysis.

Experiments report substantially lower distance-preservation error than existing dimensionality reduction methods. Used for data whitening, HoroPCA improves downstream classification by up to 3.9% compared with methods without whitening. The authors also demonstrate two-dimensional visualization of hyperbolic data. These results connect the geometric formulation to practical uses in compression, preprocessing, and visual inspection.
icml-2021-horopca-hyperbolic-dimensional.tldr: HoroPCA generalizes PCA to hyperbolic space, improving distance preservation and supporting whitening and visualization.

paragraphs: Object detection datasets can contain many examples of common categories and few examples of rare ones. Resampling images can help, but an image may contain several categories at once. Increasing how often a rare-category image is selected can therefore also increase exposure to common objects, leaving the object-level training distribution insufficiently balanced.

The paper introduces object-centered sampling through a dynamic episodic memory bank. This makes it possible to resample objects without significant additional computation. Updates to the model also provide an implicit form of feature-level augmentation. The authors combine this mechanism with image resampling, arguing that the two operate at complementary levels and both contribute to effective training.

The joint strategy achieves state-of-the-art performance on rare LVIS categories in the reported evaluation. Relative improvements over Forest R-CNN are 1.89% for detection and 3.13% for instance segmentation. The results support addressing imbalance at the object level as well as the image level, particularly when multiple categories share the same training images.
icml-2021-image-level-or-object-level-a-.tldr: Combining image resampling with memory-based object resampling improves detection and segmentation of rare categories.

paragraphs: This paper studies episodic reinforcement learning when an adversary can corrupt both rewards and transition probabilities, with the corruption unknown to the learner. In the tabular setting, the authors develop algorithms with improved regret bounds. Regret measures the performance cost accumulated while learning, so these bounds describe how corruption affects that cost.

The guarantees improve how corruption enters the analysis in two ways. They use the numerical amounts of reward and transition corruption, rather than simply counting episodes containing corruption. They also make the corruption contribution additive with respect to the smaller of √T and PolicyGapComplexity, where previous results had a multiplicative relationship. This yields a more precise dependence on the adversary's interference.

The algorithms arise from a framework combining corruption-robust policy elimination with reward-free exploration components. This separates the mechanism for managing candidate policies from the mechanism for gathering information. The authors suggest that replacing either component may extend the framework to other structured corruption settings; this is presented as a possible extension, not an established guarantee.
icml-2021-improved-corruption-robust-alg.tldr: New tabular reinforcement-learning algorithms provide sharper regret guarantees under unknown reward and transition corruption.

paragraphs: Learning a causal graph becomes more complicated when some relevant variables are unobserved. This paper focuses on ancestral acyclic directed mixed graphs, a model class used to represent causal relationships in that setting. Existing score-based approaches for these graphs are described as heuristic, leaving open whether the best-scoring graph has actually been found.

The authors formulate structure learning as an integer programming problem that returns a score-maximizing ancestral graph. Their method applies to continuous variables following a multivariate Gaussian distribution. It extends an integer programming formulation for directed acyclic graphs and introduces new valid inequalities to express the additional requirements of mixed-graph learning.

Experiments show that the formulation can be solved efficiently for medium-sized problems and achieves better accuracy than the compared score-based and constraint-based methods. The exactness claim concerns maximizing the chosen score within the specified graph class and distributional setting. This provides an optimization guarantee alongside empirical accuracy results, rather than treating a heuristic search result as necessarily optimal.
icml-2021-integer-programming-for-causal.tldr: An integer programming formulation exactly maximizes a causal-graph score for Gaussian continuous variables with latent-variable structure.

paragraphs: Transaction networks contain information that banks must analyze, but extracting useful features often requires manual expertise. Gradient flow models offer a way to learn node representations directly from transaction data through node potentials. The paper identifies two obstacles: ordinary gradient models cannot represent every graph flow, and standard fitting methods struggle with extreme values and widely varying transaction scales.

The authors extend the gradient model with gating and prove that the resulting model is a universal approximator for graph flows. They also introduce a loss based on the Student-t log-likelihood to handle multiple scales and outliers. These changes address different needs: expressive capacity for the flow model and robust fitting for transaction data.

On Ethereum transactions, gradient models achieve lower relative error than MLP models using hand-engineered or node2vec features. The results extend to 60 synthetic datasets. Additional experiments show that the gated model captures qualitative information about the synthetic flow-generating distributions, suggesting that its learned representations reflect aspects of the processes producing the observed transactions.
icml-2021-learning-node-representations-.tldr: A gated gradient model and robust loss learn transaction-network representations while accommodating general flows, outliers, and large scale differences.

paragraphs: The actions available to a reinforcement-learning agent shape what it can learn. Actions need effects large enough to evaluate, while retaining enough detail for flexible behavior. Choosing those actions and their execution frequency has traditionally required substantial manual decisions. This paper proposes learning a higher-level action space to reduce that design burden.

The new action space consists of routines. Each routine represents a set of equivalent sequences of granular actions, and those sequences can have arbitrary lengths. The routine space is learned end to end around the underlying off-policy learning objective. This ties the construction of higher-level behavior directly to the task rather than treating action grouping as a separate fixed choice.

The authors apply the framework to two leading off-policy algorithms. The resulting agents show performance improvements while requiring fewer interactions with the environment per episode, improving computational efficiency. These findings support learning the level at which an agent chooses behavior as a useful part of the reinforcement-learning problem itself.
icml-2021-learning-routines-for-effectiv.tldr: Agents learn higher-level routines of granular actions, improving off-policy learning performance and reducing interactions per episode.

paragraphs: Sequential recommendation uses a person's behavior history to anticipate future choices, but interests change over time. The paper identifies two shortcomings of existing attention mechanisms: they can overlook continuous time gaps between behaviors, and they often distribute attention broadly over the history. This is problematic when only a small part of that history is relevant to the next action.

The authors propose self-modulating attention to model preferences that evolve in complex, nonlinear ways. The approach brings temporal dynamics into the attention-based representation of behavior. Its motivation is that relevance depends on more than relationships among past actions: when those actions occurred and which ones matter to the current prediction also deserve attention.

Evaluation focuses on top-N sequential recommendation, where the model produces a ranked selection of candidate items. Results on three large real-world datasets show that the method can achieve state-of-the-art performance. The findings support the usefulness of modeling changing preferences within attention, with the performance claim grounded in the recommendation datasets studied.
icml-2021-learning-self-modulating-atten.tldr: Self-modulating attention models evolving user preferences and achieves strong results on sequential recommendation datasets.

paragraphs: This paper studies k-means clustering under local differential privacy with only one round of communication. The non-interactive requirement rules out repeated exchanges as the clustering procedure develops. The central question is whether strong clustering approximations remain possible while meeting both this communication restriction and the local privacy requirement.

The authors provide an algorithm whose approximation ratio can be made arbitrarily close to that of the best non-private approximation algorithm. This improves on previously known methods with large constant approximation ratios. They also establish the first constant-factor approximation for k-means using a single round in the local privacy model, resolving the stated open question.

The result concerns approximation quality relative to non-private algorithms, rather than a claim of always recovering the exact optimal clustering. The same framework also yields a similar near-optimal approximation in the one-round shuffle privacy model. This extension shows that the underlying approach can support strong clustering guarantees across more than one privacy setting while retaining a non-interactive communication structure.
icml-2021-locally-private-k-means-in-one.tldr: A one-round private k-means algorithm approaches the approximation ratio of the best non-private algorithm.

paragraphs: Mandoline estimates how a model will perform in a new deployment setting using labeled source data and unlabeled target data. Standard importance weighting can support this task, but it struggles with high-dimensional data or source and target distributions whose supports do not overlap. The paper uses practitioner knowledge to guide the weighting process.

Users supply simple binary slicing functions intended to capture possible directions of distribution shift. These functions can be noisy and correlated, making them a flexible way to express imperfect knowledge about differences between settings. Mandoline estimates density ratios using the slices and uses those estimates to reweight measured performance.

The authors analyze how estimation error depends on slice quality and dataset size, connecting the usefulness of the supplied knowledge to the resulting evaluation. Experiments on language and vision tasks find target-performance estimates up to three times more accurate than standard baselines. This supports guided weighting as a practical evaluation tool when target labels are unavailable, while retaining dependence on the information captured by the slices.
icml-2021-mandoline-model-evaluation-und.tldr: Mandoline uses practitioner-defined slices to improve estimates of model performance on an unlabeled target distribution.

paragraphs: Transferring behavior to a new task may require changing only a few previously successful decisions. This motivates learning procedures that can update one decision mechanism independently of others. The paper gives this notion of modular credit assignment a formal definition, focusing on how much algorithmic information different decisions' feedback signals share.

The authors introduce a modularity criterion based on causal analysis of the learning algorithm itself. They also generalize a societal decision-making framework to describe decisions more finely than a Markov decision process. For decision sequences without cycles, they prove that certain single-step temporal-difference action-value methods satisfy the criterion, whereas all policy-gradient methods fail it.

The absence of cycles is an explicit condition on that theoretical comparison. Empirical evidence further suggests that the qualifying action-value methods use samples more efficiently on transfer problems requiring sparse changes to previously optimal decision sequences. The contribution links a formal property of feedback signals to a specific kind of transfer, rather than asserting general superiority across reinforcement-learning tasks.
icml-2021-modularity-in-reinforcement-le.tldr: A formal modularity criterion distinguishes how reinforcement-learning methods assign credit and helps explain performance on sparse-change transfer tasks.

paragraphs: Neural implicit functions can represent multiple 3D shapes through a shared network conditioned on compact latent codes. Interpolating those codes produces smooth transitions between shapes, but the global transition does not directly identify how individual points correspond. This paper studies that local question by matching features within the implicit representation.

The method tracks continuous point trajectories as the latent code changes between shapes. These trajectories provide evidence for a hierarchy inside the network: earlier layers associate the code with coarse shape structure, while deeper layers refine details. Feature matching therefore serves both as a tool for following local changes and as a way to investigate what different network depths represent.

The authors also use this structured feature space for shape deformation. They report handling inconsistencies in topology and semantics, including a transition from an armchair to a chair without arms. The approach does so without explicit flow functions or manual annotations, showing how internal implicit features can support local correspondence even when the shapes differ structurally.
icml-2021-neural-feature-matching-in-imp.tldr: Matching features inside implicit 3D networks tracks point motion between shapes and supports deformation across structural differences.

paragraphs: Many graph generators construct a graph by adding nodes and edges in sequence. That process assigns an order to nodes, even though a graph can admit many such orders. Computing the graph's likelihood requires accounting for those possibilities, and their factorial growth makes direct maximum-likelihood training difficult.

The paper derives an expression for graph likelihood and connects its calculation to graph automorphism. It then develops a variational inference algorithm that maximizes a lower bound on log-likelihood. This lets training use node orderings drawn from an approximate posterior, giving the choice of ordering a probabilistic basis rather than relying on an ad hoc sequence.

Experiments find that the resulting log-likelihood bound is significantly tighter than bounds from previous schemes. Models trained this way also generate high-quality graphs whose structures match target graphs absent from training. The findings connect more careful treatment of node order to both improved likelihood approximation and useful graph generation, while retaining an approximate inference procedure.
icml-2021-order-matters-probabilistic-mo.tldr: Variational inference learns probabilistically grounded node orderings for graph generation and produces tighter likelihood bounds.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement-learning research often evaluates new methods on established environments such as Atari games. These benchmarks provide common comparison points, but their computational demands can make participation harder for researchers with limited resources. This paper examines whether smaller, traditional environments can still support useful scientific investigation while lowering those barriers.

The authors revisit the empirical study that introduced Rainbow and investigate the algorithms it uses. Their purpose is to demonstrate that studying familiar methods at a smaller scale can reveal meaningful insights. The paper therefore treats the choice of experimental environment as part of research design, with consequences for both what can be learned and who can participate.

The empirical revisit produces new insights into Rainbow's component algorithms, supporting the argument that small-scale environments remain scientifically valuable. The abstract does not claim that these environments replace every role of larger benchmarks. Its stated contribution is evidence that useful reinforcement-learning research can also be conducted in settings with more accessible computational requirements.
icml-2021-revisiting-rainbow-promoting-m.tldr: Revisiting Rainbow shows that small-scale environments can yield useful reinforcement-learning insights while lowering computational barriers.

paragraphs: A Wasserstein barycenter represents a weighted average of probability distributions using optimal-transport geometry. This paper develops an approximation algorithm aimed at high-dimensional machine-learning applications. The goal is to make this distributional averaging practical while preserving a formulation based on how probability mass is transported between distributions.

The algorithm combines the Kantorovich dual formulation of the Wasserstein-2 distance with input convex neural networks, which parameterize convex functions. It requires samples from the input distributions rather than a more explicit description of them. The barycenter itself is represented by a generative model, making the result a distribution from which new samples can be drawn.

Once learned, the generator can produce arbitrarily many barycenter samples without querying the original distributions again. With only one input distribution, the method behaves similarly to a generative adversarial model. Comparisons with state-of-the-art methods across multiple experiments demonstrate its efficacy. The contribution joins an optimal-transport objective with a reusable generative representation of the approximate average distribution.
icml-2021-scalable-computations-of-wasse.tldr: Input convex neural networks enable a sample-based Wasserstein barycenter algorithm that learns a reusable generative model.

paragraphs: Controlling an anthropomorphic robotic hand involves coordinating complex movements during object manipulation. This paper introduces challenging simulated tasks on which current reinforcement-learning and trajectory-optimization methods perform poorly. The suite includes passing or throwing objects between two hands and spinning a long pen between a hand's fingers.

The authors first develop a simple trajectory-optimization algorithm that performs significantly better than existing approaches on these environments. They then focus on PenSpin, identified as the most difficult task. For that task, trajectory optimization produces demonstrations that are useful even though they are suboptimal, and those demonstrations are combined with off-policy reinforcement learning.

The combined method achieves performance far beyond either trajectory optimization or reinforcement learning alone on PenSpin. This result shows that imperfect optimized demonstrations can complement learning in a demanding manipulation setting. The paper contributes both a challenging simulated task suite and evidence for combining the two approaches, with the strongest stated combination result tied specifically to pen spinning.
icml-2021-solving-challenging-dexterous-.tldr: Combining suboptimal trajectory-optimization demonstrations with off-policy learning substantially improves simulated pen-spinning performance.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised classification can encounter both incorrect labels and outlying inputs. This paper develops a unified robust semi-supervised variational autoencoder, URSVAE, to address these two forms of noise together. The motivation is that protecting a model against only one source of contamination leaves the other able to distort learning.

The model places uncertainty priors on parameters of probability distributions to improve the encoder's robustness to outliers. A noise-transition model addresses label errors, while a robust divergence measure adds another source of protection. The authors derive a new variational lower bound and optimize it to learn the network parameters within the combined framework.

The analysis proves that the influence function of the proposed evidence lower bound is bounded, providing a specific theoretical robustness property. Image-classification experiments report superiority over the compared state-of-the-art approaches. Together, the analysis and experiments support jointly modeling outliers and noisy labels, without turning bounded influence into a claim that arbitrary combinations of noise can always be overcome.
icml-2021-unified-robust-semi-supervised.tldr: URSVAE jointly addresses noisy labels and outliers through uncertainty modeling, label-noise transitions, and a robust training objective.

paragraphs: Learning control from images depends heavily on how visual information is represented. Structured representations such as keypoints can help, but many existing approaches learn them in two dimensions even when the agent acts in a three-dimensional world. This paper learns a 3D keypoint representation directly from images to better align visual structure with the control setting.

A differentiable encoder maps input images into latent 3D keypoints. Training combines a multi-view consistency loss with the downstream task objective, so the representation is shaped by both geometric agreement and its usefulness for control. The framework learns this structure end to end in an unsupervised manner, without relying on manually specified keypoint identities.

The discovered keypoints tend to track robot joints and object motion consistently across time and 3D space. Across a variety of reinforcement-learning benchmarks, the approach outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods. The findings support using learned spatial structure as part of visual control, while the correspondence to meaningful joints and movements remains an observed tendency.
icml-2021-unsupervised-learning-of-visua.tldr: Learning consistent 3D keypoints directly from images improves visual control across evaluated reinforcement-learning benchmarks.
